query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled low‐temperature aging treatment that induces a fine, high-density dispersion of coherent L12 precipitates within the FCC lamellae of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA will improve its long-term performance by enhancing creep resistance and stabilizing the passive film against corrosion during extreme temperature cycling, while maintaining an acceptable strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA with a uniform, fine lamellar mixture of FCC and B2 phases.
generation.intervention: Apply an optimized low-temperature aging heat treatment (e.g., around 580°C for 24 hours) to induce nano-scale, coherent L12 intermetallic precipitates within the FCC lamellae.
generation.conditions: Service environments featuring cyclic thermal fluctuations (room temperature to ~700°C), sustained mechanical loading (including room-temperature creep), and corrosive challenges (e.g., chloride-containing environments typical for aerospace applications).
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale, coherent L12 precipitates uniformly distributed in the ductile FCC lamellae.
generation.mechanism: The coherent L12 particles act as effective barriers to dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding, thereby increasing the yield strength and slowing creep deformation. Their stable and chemically robust nature also helps in maintaining an intact and adherent passive oxide film under thermal cycling, which reduces the susceptibility to corrosion and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated or conventionally processed alloy, the aged alloy is expected to show an increase in tensile yield strength (on the order of ~200 MPa improvement), enhanced creep resistance (lower steady-state creep rates under similar loads), and improved corrosion stability (more stable passive films and reduced pitting) under cyclic thermal and mechanical stress while retaining sufficient ductility (around 13–15% elongation).
generation.baseline: The starting material’s performance is characterized by a fine lamellar FCC/B2 structure with yield strengths around 770–990 MPa (depending on processing) but with observed limitations in sustained creep performance and passive film stability under extreme temperature fluctuations and corrosive environments.
generation.boundary: This improvement is anticipated only if the aging treatment is precisely controlled to yield a fine dispersion of L12 precipitates; excessive aging or coarsening may negate benefits by compromising ductility or triggering embrittlement, and the benefits must be validated within the specified temperature and loading regimes.
generation.uncertainty: While prior work (e.g., PMC6478865 and PMC4145285) has demonstrated that L12 precipitation can enhance strength with minimal ductility loss under quasi-static and dynamic conditions, it is uncertain how the precipitate distribution and its barrier effects will evolve under long-term, cyclic thermal/mechanical loading and in corrosive environments. This hypothesis extends those findings to address creep and corrosion under aerospace-relevant conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA samples: one group to receive the optimized low-temperature aging treatment (580°C for 24 h) to induce L12 precipitation, and a control group with conventional processing (as-cast or cold-rolled without aging). Subject both groups to cyclic thermal treatment (cycling between room temperature and ~700°C), sustained mechanical creep tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures, and corrosion tests in chloride-containing acidic solutions.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ultimate tensile strength (via quasi-static tensile tests)
Creep strain rate and time to failure under constant load (via creep tests)
Microstructural stability and precipitate morphology evolution (via TEM/SEM analyses before and after cyclic treatments)
Corrosion performance (via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, potentiodynamic polarization, and pitting density analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., <~100–200 MPa increase in yield strength, no decrease in creep strain rate, or no improvement in corrosion resistance metrics compared to the control) under the cyclic thermal and mechanical test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The YHf co-doping did not alter the solidification microstructure and phase structure of the EHEA coating. The microstructure morphologies of the top and bottom portions of coatings were composed of cellular and columnar dendrites, respectively. And the phase structure consisted of FCC and BCC/B2. 2. After heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h, the BCC/B2 structure was relatively stable in all coatings while the nanoscale Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC. 3. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. Recent studies indicate that eutectic high-entropy alloys can simultaneously possess high strength and high ductility, which have potential industrial applications. The present study focuses on Al0.7CoCrFeNi, a lamellar dual-phase (fcc + B2) precipitation-strengthenable eutectic high entropy alloy. This alloy exhibits an fcc + B2 (B2 with bcc nano-precipitates) microstructure resulting in a combination of the soft and ductile fcc phase together with hard B2 phase. Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength. The strengthening contribution due to fine scale L12 is modeled using Orowan dislocation bowing and by-pass mechanism. The alloy was tested under quasi-static (strain-rate = 10−3 s−1) tensile loading and dynamic (strain-rate = 103 s−1) compressive loading. Due to the fine lamellar microstructure with a large number of fcc-bcc interfaces, the alloy show relatively high flow-stresses, ~1400 MPa under quasi-static loading and in excess of 1800 MPa under dynamic loading. Quasi-static tensile tests of both the heat-treated conditions was performed to evaluate the change in mechanical performance due to precipitation of the ordered L12 phase under uniaxial loading. The tensile strength of Al0.7CoCrFeNi in HTA-580 condition is higher compared to Al0.7CoCrFeNi in HTA condition (Figure 3a). The fcc + L12/bcc + B2 microstructure (HTA-580) in this alloy exhibited a tensile yield strength (YS) close to 1000 MPa (~990 MPa), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) ~ 1400 MPa and elongation to failure of ~13% while the fcc/bcc + B2 microstructure in HTA condition showed a YS of 780 MPa, UTS of ~1100 MPa and elongation to failure of 17% under quasi-static loading (strain rate of 10−3). The YS increased by 200 MPa which can be attributed to the L12 precipitates in fcc lamellae formed after the low-temperature heat treatment at 580 °C.
